newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees new path of hepatitis infection.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees new path of hepatitis infection.

text.p: A woman infected with hepatitis C inadvertently transmitted the deadly virus to her haemophiliac child with an injection of a blood clotting agent, federal health officials said on Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the case illustrated the risk of infection in families where someone with an illness is being treated at home. It said there had been no previous reported cases where hepatitis C virus had been transmitted between household members except by sexual contact.

"The mother did not know that she had hepatitis C virus infection and therefore didn't think she had to take any special precautions," CDC epidemiologist Beth Bell said. "The mother stuck herself with the needle on several occasions while attempting to do the infusion," Bell said.

Hepatitis C can be transmitted through blood or sexual contact and from a mother to a newborn infant. People most at risk for infection include injecting drug users, health-care workers, haemodialysis patients and transfusion recipients.
The CDC recommends that health workers who have been exposed to hepatitis C be tested six months later to see if they were infected.
"The risk of acquiring hepatitis C virus infection after a needlestick averages about 2 percent," Dr. Miriam Alter, chief of the epidemiology section of CDC's hepatitis branch, said.
The CDC said 8,000 to 10,000 people die every year from hepatitis C. There is no vaccine to prevent infection.
